sentences.text: Zhejiangopterus was a moderately large pterosaur.
Early measurements suggested a wingspan of 5 meters, though later studies adjusted this to roughly 3.5 meters, estimating a body mass of 7.9 kilograms.
Its skull was long and low with a perfect arch, lacking any keel or crest.
The nasal opening and antorbital fenestra merged into one single oval space that took up nearly half the skull's length.
The first six dorsal vertebrae fused together to form a notarium.
The femur was thin and long, measuring 1.5 times the length of the humerus.
By the early 1990s, six large fossils had been recovered from the 81.5 million-year-old Tangshang Formation.
A quarry worker named Xu Chengfa discovered the first fossil of Zhejiangopterus in April 1986 near the village of Aolicun in Linhai.
The discoverer Xu Chengfa found three additional specimens before dying in an accident in 1988, while another worker later found a complete skull.
The genus was named in 1994 by Chinese paleontologists Cai Zhengquan and Wei Feng.
The genus name refers to Zhejiang Province and the Latinized Greek word for 'wing'.
Original describers classified Zhejiangopterus in Nyctosauridae due to its resemblance to the toothless Nyctosaurus.
In 1997, David Unwin reclassified Zhejiangopterus into Azhdarchidae based on its relationship to Quetzalcoatlus.
Zhejiangopterus is classified in the family Azhdarchidae.
The genus authority is Cai & Feng, 1994.
The type species is Zhejiangopterus linhaiensis, described by Cai & Feng in 1994.
A cladogram placing Zhejiangopterus within Neoazhdarchia was recovered by Brian Andres and Timothy Myers in 2013.
Zhejiangopterus lived in China during the late Cretaceous Period.
Zhejiangopterus lived between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago during the Campanian stage.
